title: GDPR
summary: The General Data Protection Regulation is the European Union legal framework governing the processing of personal data, and it applies to organisations established in the EU as well as organisations outside the EU that offer goods or services to, or monitor the behaviour of, people in the EU. Its obligations are built on principles rather than prescriptive controls: lawfulness, fairness and transparency; purpose limitation; data minimisation; accuracy; storage limitation; integrity and confidentiality; and accountability, where the organisation must be able to demonstrate compliance rather than merely assert it. For security practitioners the regulation matters in four operational areas. Article 32 requires appropriate technical and organisational measures proportionate to risk, which is where encryption, pseudonymisation, access control, resilience and testing of those measures land. Articles 33 and 34 set breach notification duties, with a seventy-two hour window to the supervisory authority once the controller becomes aware, so incident response runbooks must be able to answer what data, how many people, what categories and what residual risk within hours. Chapter IV introduces the data protection impact assessment for high-risk processing and the records of processing activities that underpin it. Chapter V governs transfers outside the EU and drives data residency, standard contractual clauses and transfer impact assessments. The security team's artefact trail, including detection records, containment timelines and post-incident reviews, is frequently the evidence that a supervisory authority examines.
objectives: You will be able to map the data protection principles onto concrete engineering and operational controls.
You will be able to determine what Article 32 appropriate measures mean for a given processing activity and risk level.
You will be able to run a breach assessment that produces the information a seventy-two hour notification requires.
You will be able to support a data protection impact assessment with accurate data flow and risk evidence.
You will be able to explain how international transfer restrictions change architecture and vendor selection.
You will be able to identify where a controller and a processor hold different obligations in an incident.

beginner.definition: The General Data Protection Regulation is a European Union law about personal data. Personal data means any information that can identify a living person. The law says how organisations may collect, use, store and share that information. It also gives people rights over their own data.
beginner.whyItMatters: If you handle data about people in Europe, this law applies even when your company sits elsewhere. A serious breach can lead to large fines and to lost trust. The law also sets a deadline, because you may need to tell a regulator within seventy-two hours of learning about a breach. That means your incident notes must be clear and fast to produce.
howItWorks: Decide why you need each piece of personal data and write that reason down.
Collect only what the reason requires, and delete it when the reason ends.
Protect the data with strong encryption, limited access and tested recovery plans.
Keep clear records showing what personal data you hold and where it flows.
If a breach happens, assess the risk to people and notify within the deadline.
Give people a way to see, correct and delete their own information.
beginner.example: Think of a gym that keeps member details. The gym needs your name and payment to bill you, but it does not need your medical history to sell a membership. If someone steals the membership list, the gym must work out how many people are affected and how serious the harm is. Then it may have to inform the privacy regulator quickly. Keeping less data made that job smaller.
takeaways: Collect the smallest amount of personal data that your purpose needs.
Know your breach deadline and keep evidence ready before you need it.
People have rights over their data, so build ways to answer them.

exercises.title: GDPR - EASY
exercises.summary: Recall and recognition: definitions, one clear answer, single-step questions.

exercises.title: GDPR - MEDIUM
exercises.summary: Application: read a short log or alert and choose the correct next step.

exercises.title: GDPR - HARD
exercises.summary: Analysis: a multi-step scenario with distractors, evidence to weigh, and a reason to give.

exercises.title: GDPR - EXTREMELY HARD
exercises.summary: Synthesis under pressure: incomplete evidence, competing priorities, and a decision you must defend.
